opus-5.5.text:
I think Carlos's advice was one of the most valuable things I got during my PhD, and the more time passes, the more I appreciate it.

The core of it was that when you commit to a direction, you shouldn't stop at the first paper. It's easy, especially early on, to treat research as a series of separate projects: find a problem, write a paper, move on. Carlos pushed me to go much deeper, to keep at a direction until you really understand it end to end and have built something people can actually use. Not just a clever idea, but the whole stack: the algorithm, the system, the implementation details, and how real users run into it.

Looking back, that's how XGBoost happened. Gradient boosting wasn't a new idea. What made a difference was digging into all the parts people usually skip: sparsity handling, cache-aware access, distributed computation, and making it robust enough for people to rely on in competitions and in industry. None of that would have come from a "publish and move on" mindset. The same goes for TVM and the machine learning compilation work later. Those problems only reveal their interesting structure once you've lived with them for years.

I'd add one caveat from my own experience. Going deep doesn't mean going narrow or being stubborn. You still need to pick a direction where depth pays off, ideally where there's a real gap and real demand. And as you go deeper, you naturally connect to neighboring areas. For me, going deep on systems for machine learning pulled me into compilers, hardware, and now large model deployment. So depth is what earns you breadth over time.

My overall assessment is that it's very good advice, especially in a field that moves this fast. Everyone is chasing the next trend, so the people who stay with a problem long enough to really own it end up having outsized impact. It takes some patience and conviction, because the payoff isn't immediate, but I think it's worth it.

fable-5.1.text:
Carlos—Carlos Guestrin—was my advisor at University of Washington, and the advice he gave me about depth was something I resisted at first, honestly. When I started as a PhD student I had this instinct to spread out. I wanted to touch systems, touch machine learning theory, touch applications, because every one of those directions looked exciting and I didn't want to miss anything.

What Carlos told me was essentially: pick one thing and go all the way down. Not depth in the sense of reading everything that has been published, but depth in the sense of becoming the person who actually built the thing end to end, understands every failure mode, and knows why each design decision was made. His framing was that breadth will come naturally later, but depth is something you have to deliberately protect, because the pull toward the next shiny problem is always there.

Looking back, I think he was mostly right, with one qualification. The part that was right is that XGBoost, and later MXNet and TVM, only happened because I stayed on a problem long after the point where it would have been reasonable to say "okay, this works, let's move on." The interesting engineering and the interesting research questions only showed up once the easy version was done and I had to make it fast, make it scale, make it usable for people who were not me. If I had switched directions every year I would have written several okay papers and never built anything that people actually use.

The qualification is that depth in one direction eventually forces you to go wide anyway. To make gradient boosting fast I had to learn about cache behavior and distributed systems. To make TVM work I had to learn compilers, which I had not planned on. So I would describe my own path less as "depth versus breadth" and more as depth first, and then let the problem pull you into adjacent areas when it demands it. That's a different kind of breadth than sampling topics from the outside. It's breadth earned by necessity, and it tends to stick.

So my assessment is that Carlos's advice is the right default for a young researcher, and the main thing I would add is to pick a direction where the depth has somewhere to go—where solving it properly will inevitably teach you things outside your starting field. If the problem is deep enough, the breadth takes care of itself.

astra-6.text: I think Carlos’s advice is valuable because there’s a big difference between trying an idea and really understanding a research direction. When you commit to a problem, you want to go deep enough to understand why an approach works, where it fails, and what the underlying challenges are. That takes time, and sometimes the interesting insights come after the obvious things don’t work. But depth doesn’t mean sticking with something forever. It means giving yourself enough understanding to make a thoughtful decision about whether to keep going or change direction.

sol-6.1.text: I think the spirit of Carlos’s advice is that, once you choose a direction, you should be willing to go deep enough to develop your own understanding of it. If you stop at the first obstacle, you may never reach the interesting part. But depth doesn’t mean continuing blindly. As you learn more, you should keep asking whether the problem matters and whether your approach still makes sense. I see it as a commitment to understanding the problem, rather than a commitment to defending your original idea.
